children: AAHL plans to expand non-aeronautical and city-side businesses to reduce its regulated revenue profile to single digits

Adani Airports Holding (AAHL) is working on a strategy to bring regulatory charges at its airports down to the bare minimum by expanding non-aeronautical businesses and city-side development, CEO Arun Bansal said.

Speaking at the 13th SBI Banking and Economics Conclave 2026, Bansal said the company's ambition is to make the regulated revenue base significantly smaller by growing businesses beyond core airport operations. He said the aim is to bring the regulatory revenue profile down to almost single digits over time.

Aeronautical charges are fees associated with the direct use of core airport and terminal infrastructure, while non-aeronautical revenue comes from activities such as retail, leasing, food and beverage, advertising and other commercial services.
Bansal said the strategy involves increasing the contribution from non-aeronautical and city-side development businesses, allowing airports to rely less on regulated revenue.

At present, aeronautical charges account for a significant share of AAHL's revenue. Bansal said that last year, around 60% of revenue across its eight airports came from aeronautical activities, with the balance generated through non-aeronautical businesses. By 2030, the company expects the revenue mix to shift, with around 70% coming from non-aeronautical sources.
Navi Mumbai Airport Positioned As Potential Hub

Bansal also highlighted Navi Mumbai International Airport, which has been planned and developed with the ambition of becoming an international hub once an Indian carrier begins operating direct flights to Europe or the US from the airport.
He said the airport has been built with the infrastructure required to support such a role, while other Indian airports could also develop as international hubs.

Bansal said India's ability to emerge as a global aviation hub will also depend on the growth of Indian airlines. He pointed to the aircraft orders placed by IndiGo and Air India, saying that once these aircraft are delivered, India could have greater capacity to develop international hubs.

The Adani Airports CEO also said the operator plans to begin demolishing Terminal 1 at Mumbai International Airport from January 15, 2027. Traffic will be redistributed between Terminal 2 and Navi Mumbai International Airport as the redevelopment progresses.

Around five million passengers currently associated with Terminal 1's capacity will need to be accommodated elsewhere during the redevelopment, he said. Airlines, however, will decide whether to shift their operations between Mumbai and Navi Mumbai airports.
Bansal said the operator cannot compel airlines to move their services to a particular airport, adding that carriers have been given time to plan their operations around the redevelopment.

Bansal also said Adani Airports is focused on developing airport infrastructure rather than entering the airline business. The company, he said, needs to expand its airport capacity substantially over the coming decade.

The strategy of increasing non-aeronautical and city-side revenue is therefore being pursued alongside investments in airport infrastructure and the development of Navi Mumbai as a potential international aviation hub.
